text: You've spent this course learning the pieces: Python basics, NumPy, pandas, cleaning, files and databases, and reliable-code habits. The capstone puts them together on one project, start to finish, the way a working data scientist would. Real company data can't be shared, so we generate an illustrative retail orders file with NumPy and pandas — deliberately built with the problems real exports have.

Imagine you've joined an online home-and-lifestyle shop, and the head of sales asks: where does our revenue come from, and are our discounts actually working? That's too vague to code, so we sharpen it into two questions — which regions, categories, and months drive revenue, and do heavily discounted orders contain more items and come back more often. We also define the metric before looking at data: revenue equals quantity times unit price times one minus discount, counted only for complete orders.

The project folder keeps raw data in data slash raw, never edited, and cleaned data in data slash clean, with a cleaning module, tests, an analysis notebook, and a README. make_data.py generates the practice file: fifteen hundred rows from a seeded random generator, with a busier fourth quarter and returns that rise with discount size — relationships we planted on purpose so there's something real to find.

Then the script deliberately makes it messy: thirty percent of dates switch to US format, some regions get uppercased or padded with spaces, some prices pick up a dollar sign, a few quantities and discounts go missing, six rows get absurd quantities like 999 or negative two, and thirty duplicate rows get appended. Notice the reproducibility habits already at work — a seeded generator, pathlib, no hard-coded paths.

Before touching anything, audit the raw file: its shape comes out to 1,530 rows and 9 columns, with 30 fully duplicated rows. Missing values show up in region, quantity, and discount_pct. order_date and unit_price are stored as text, with prices sometimes carrying a dollar sign and dates arriving in two different formats. Region appears as North, NORTH, and padded with spaces; status as complete and Complete. And quantities include 999, 500, and 250, alongside 0, -1, and -2.

Every finding becomes a written decision before you code: drop exact duplicates; standardize region and status text, labeling missing region Unknown; convert prices to numbers and parse both date formats; keep only quantities from 1 to 20, a business rule you'd confirm with the shop, and drop missing quantities since revenue can't be computed; treat a missing discount as 0 but flag those rows; then add revenue and month columns.

To recap: sharpen a vague request into specific questions and a defined metric, keep raw data untouched and audit it thoroughly before cleaning, and turn every problem you find into a written cleaning decision. Next lesson, we build it — turning this plan into tested code and real answers.
